To fix a broken system, one must understand the extent of the failure. In this case, what is broken is approximately everything.

They say knowledge is power. But in this case, knowledge is mostly just depressing. Still, it is necessary.

## Daily Numbers

Every single day, {{< var global_daily_deaths_curable_diseases >}} humans stop existing because of diseases society could probably cure if anyone was paying attention (nobody is).

Visualizing {{< var global_daily_deaths_curable_diseases >}} people is difficult. It is like taking everyone in a decent-sized stadium and removing them. Then doing it again tomorrow. And the day after that. Forever. One would run out of stadiums before running out of corpses, which seems like poor urban planning.

That is fifty 9/11s. Per day. Every day. Including weekends and holidays.

After the first 9/11, America invaded two countries and spent $2 trillion. After the fifty daily 9/11s, humanity shrugs and wonders what is for lunch.

When one thing kills 3,000 people, it is a tragedy and nations start wars. When diseases kill 50 times that every day, it is called "natural causes," which is Latin for "society couldn't be bothered".

If aliens were studying humanity, they would probably conclude humans cannot count past 3,000.

## Where the Money Goes

Here is how humanity allocates its resources:

**Killing each other:** {{< var global_military_spending_annual_2024 >}} per year
**Curing diseases:** {{< var global_med_research_spending >}} per year

But the real bottleneck is not research funding. It is testing which treatments actually work. Clinical trials determine whether medicines save lives or sit on shelves. On that front, governments worldwide spend {{< var global_government_clinical_trials_spending_annual >}} annually on clinical trials versus {{< var global_military_spending_annual_2024 >}} on weapons. That is a {{< var military_to_government_clinical_trials_spending_ratio >}}:1 ratio, which in technical terms is called "having priorities backwards."

For comparison, imagine if a household spent $2,700 on guns and $68 on food. The neighbors would stage an intervention (or call the police, or possibly just move). But when humanity does it, nations call it "military spending" and give everyone medals.

## On Military Accounting

The Pentagon has lost $2.5 trillion. Not spent. Lost. Like car keys, except the car keys could cure cancer several hundred times.

When individuals lose $20, they search the couch cushions. When the Pentagon loses $2,500,000,000,000, they ask for more money and Congress says yes.

If citizens tried this with taxes, they would be arrested. When the military does it, it is called "standard operating procedure," which is also Latin, probably for "we are making this up as we go."

They say a trillion is just a number. But it is the number of dollars lost that could have funded medical research for thirty-seven years. Give or take a few hospitals, several cancer cures, and maybe a solution to aging (but who needs that when nations have seventeen redundant aircraft carrier strike groups).

## On Medical Research

Since 1970, the National Institutes of Health has spent over $1 trillion studying diseases.

Diseases cured: Zero.

Well, technically that is not fair. They cured... upon checking the notes... no, it is zero.

To be clear, they have learned lots of interesting things about how diseases work. They just have not gotten around to the part where people stop dying from them. It is like spending fifty years studying how cars work without ever actually driving anywhere (researchers just publish papers about theoretical carburetor optimization while everyone walks to work).

The NIH tests about 5,000 treatment combinations per year. There are 166 billion possible combinations. At this rate, they will be done by the year 33,200,000. Mark the calendars (use pencil, timelines may shift due to budget constraints and the eventual heat death of the universe).

## On the FDA

The FDA is the American mechanism for ensuring drug safety. They do this by making the approval process so expensive and slow that most drugs never get approved at all.

It takes {{< var treatment_acceleration_years_current >}} years and $2.6 billion to get a drug through FDA approval. {{< var treatment_acceleration_years_current >}} years. That is longer than it took to build the pyramids, and those involved moving rocks the size of houses without machinery (also the pharaohs did not have to file quarterly progress reports in triplicate).

During the Oxford RECOVERY trial, researchers tested treatments on 40,000 patients for {{< var recovery_trial_cost_per_patient >}} per person. The FDA's process costs {{< var traditional_phase3_cost_per_patient_fda_example_41k >}} per patient. That is {{< var trial_cost_reduction_factor >}} times more expensive for the same result, except slower. It is like getting a haircut for $10 or $820, but the $820 haircut takes {{< var treatment_acceleration_years_current >}} years and the patient might be bald by then anyway.

Ninety-five percent of diseases have zero approved treatments. This is because the FDA is very good at preventing bad drugs from reaching people, and also pretty good at preventing good drugs from reaching people, and absolutely excellent at preventing any drugs from reaching people.

They say the road to hell is paved with good intentions. The FDA's road is paved with good intentions and also {{< var treatment_acceleration_years_current >}} years of bureaucracy.

## On What War Costs

Humanity spends {{< var global_military_spending_annual_2024 >}} every year on war. That works out to {{< var global_military_spending_per_capita_annual >}} per human on Earth for death tools.

This budget includes:

- Nuclear bombs (13,000 of them, because 12,999 would not destroy Earth thoroughly enough)
- Bullets (many)
- AI murder robots (the future is here and it is disappointing)
- Fighter jets that cost more than hospitals
- Submarines (one submarine = 1,000 cancer research labs)
- Probably some kind of earthquake machine

The average personal lifetime contribution to the murder budget is $74,259. One could have bought a really nice casket instead.

The interesting thing about having 13,000 nuclear warheads is that after the first few hundred, nations are just showing off. It is like having 13,000 fire extinguishers in a kitchen. After a while, one is not worried about fires, one is just collecting them.

## On What Disease Costs

Disease extracts {{< var global_disease_economic_burden_annual >}} from humanity annually. That is trillion with a T, which stands for "that is an unconscionably large number."

This includes:

- $8.2 trillion on healthcare (treating symptoms because cures are bad for business)
- $100.9 trillion in economic losses (dead people are notoriously unproductive)
- 10 million cancer deaths per year (cancer: 10 million, humanity: 0)
- 2 billion people with chronic diseases (occurring currently)
- 1 billion depressed humans (costing $5 trillion in lost "wanting to exist")
- 95% of rare diseases with zero treatments (too rare to profit from, sorry)

{{< include figures/trial-access-disparity-chart.qmd >}}

Out of {{< var current_disease_patients_global >}} people suffering from chronic disease right now, only {{< var current_trial_slots_available >}} get to participate in clinical trials annually. That is {{< var current_patient_participation_rate >}}. The other 99.8% get to suffer and wait (and fill out insurance paperwork, and argue with the insurance company about whether dying is covered under the plan).

Half of humanity would volunteer if asked. The system turns away 99.6% of willing participants. It is like running a restaurant but only serving 0.4% of the people who want to eat there, then wondering why everyone is so hungry.

The last disease cured was Hepatitis C in 2014. The next cure is scheduled for 2064. Please wait patiently and try not to die in the meantime.

If disease were a country, it would be the richest country on Earth by a factor of ten. Unfortunately, disease does not have a flag or an army, so nobody invades it.

## On Democracy

Democracy is when everyone votes and the government does what everyone wants. At least that is what the brochure says.

In reality, a Princeton study found 0% correlation between what the public wants and what policies get enacted. Zero percent. One would get better results with a magic 8-ball.

This is because of something called "concentrated benefits versus diffuse costs." When military contractors want $100 billion, they spend $55 million lobbying for it. That is a 1,813% return on investment.

When individuals want healthcare, they have approximately zero dollars to lobby with because they spent it all on healthcare (or they are dead, which significantly reduces lobbying capacity - corpses have no political voice, despite making up the largest constituency).

Lobbying is basically legal bribery, except we call it "free speech" so it sounds nicer. It is like how "alternative facts" sounds better than "lies," or how "enhanced interrogation" sounds better than "torture."

## On Regulatory Capture

Regulatory capture is when the people who are supposed to regulate an industry used to work for that industry and will work for that industry again after they are done "regulating" it.

The process works like this:

1. Work at pharmaceutical company, learn what they want
2. Join FDA, write rules pharmaceutical company likes  
3. Return to pharmaceutical company with 400% raise
4. The circle of life is complete

The Pentagon has the same system, except with more explosions.

This is why the FDA's rules mysteriously benefit large pharmaceutical companies who can afford $2.6 billion approval processes, and why Pentagon procurement mysteriously benefits military contractors who can afford $1,800 hammers.

## On the Fixed Pie

Here is something rarely taught in economics class: Money is not real, but resources are.

Earth has 8 billion human brains. One cannot print more brains. When the government prints money for military contractors, those contractors buy the smartest people. Every MIT graduate building missiles is not curing cancer.

Medical research funding has increased 10X in dollars but decreased as a percentage of GDP. This is because governments are printing money for weapons faster than they are printing money for cures. 

The brain drain is real: Raytheon pays $150,000 to design bombs, the NIH pays $55,000 to cure diseases. It is obvious where the geniuses go.

Switzerland spends 0.7% of GDP on military and has $93,000 GDP per capita. America spends {{< var us_military_spending_pct_gdp >}} on military and has $76,000 GDP per capita. 

The solution is not to print more money for medical research. The solution is to change the ratio. Take money from the killing budget, give it to the not-dying budget. This is called "arithmetic," which is apparently a controversial field of mathematics.

## On The Human Condition

During the reading of this text, approximately 8 people have died from preventable diseases. By the end of this chapter, it will be 15.

The human body is currently:

- Growing cancer cells (slowly, hopefully)
- Forgetting memories (where was the car parked?)
- Wearing out joints (that knee is not getting better)
- Shortening telomeres (the cellular countdown clock)
- Accumulating damage (entropy is undefeated)

Humans are literally falling apart at the molecular level. Every moment one exists, one is dying slightly. It is like being a sandcastle at high tide, except slower and with more paperwork.

The technology to fix most of this exists. It is just busy building fighter jets instead.

## What This Means

To summarize:

- {{< var global_daily_deaths_curable_diseases >}} humans are deleted daily by curable diseases
- {{< var global_military_spending_annual_2024 >}} spent annually on weapons
- {{< var global_med_research_spending >}} spent annually on curing all diseases combined
- {{< var military_to_government_clinical_trials_spending_ratio >}}:1 weapons-to-clinical-trials spending ratio (the bottleneck is not research. It is testing which medicines work.)
- Zero diseases cured in 50 years
- $2.5 trillion lost by Pentagon (whoops)
- 0% correlation between public preferences and policy
- Humans are dying while reading this

If this seems bad, that is because one is paying attention.

The good news is society can fix it.

The bad news is it requires doing things.

The weird news is wealth can be generated doing it.

They say every problem is an opportunity in disguise. In this case, the opportunity is disguised as 150,000 corpses per day, which is admittedly not the most encouraging disguise, but one works with what one has.
